title: Vacuum Cup Validation for a Robot Gripper
cardSummary: Two-phase bench and field test plan for a 63-cup gripper's replacement cup
metaDescription: At Mujin I wrote the plan to qualify a replacement vacuum cup for a robot gripper and led the field trial, which caught a failure the bench tests missed.
oneLiner: I wrote the plan to qualify a replacement vacuum cup for a 63-cup robot gripper, ran the bench tests and led the field A/B at a 24/7 distribution center. The field test caught a durability failure the bench missed. After my internship ended, Mujin's on-site team applied the plan's criteria and called a no-swap before any fleet rollout.
role: Test plan author and test lead
whatIOwnedSummary: I wrote the 13-page plan on my own and designed every test in both phases. My manager and a senior technical writer reviewed and approved it. I modified the force/vacuum test jig and ran the Phase 1 bench tests on it with KEYENCE pressure sensing. I designed the decision rule, the failure triage protocol and the Service Log, and added two metrics to StatsMonitor, the fleet monitoring pipeline I built. I led the Phase 2 field test, and Mujin's on-site team carried it to the decision after my internship ended. The vendor relationship and sample procurement were outside my scope.

path.decision: Two phases: single-cup bench tests, then a warehouse A/B with checkpoints at 30, 60 and 90 days.
path.why: Catch failure modes on the bench before a long run at a customer site.

path.decision: Fixed the rule before any data came in. Piece loss rate can't get worse than the incumbent's, and the candidate has to win on at least one of four metrics chosen in advance.
path.why: So the result could be called without arguing about vendors.

path.decision: Added two of the four must-win metrics to StatsMonitor.
path.why: They didn't exist when I scoped the plan.

path.decision: Designed a backpressure check and a replacement decision tree on a fixed pick-count and time schedule, logged to a Service Log.
path.why: To keep interventions comparable across the two A/B grippers.

path.decision: Took tight stretch-wrap testing past the planned weight cap. Documented the loose stretch-wrap failure as a known risk going into Phase 2.
path.why: I wanted to find where it failed, not stop at the plan's limit. Phase 2 then ran the customer's normal line speed and package mix, not a targeted test of one surface.

path.decision: The candidate cups cracked and wore down within about two weeks. After my internship ended, Mujin's on-site team applied the plan's criteria and called a no-swap.
path.why: Staging kept it to one site instead of the fleet.

path.decision: Add a cyclic wear test and a bench A/B against clean incumbent cups to Phase 1.
path.why: Phase 1 was static and short, so the wear first showed up in the field.

claims.title: Wrote a two-phase plan to qualify a replacement vacuum cup from a candidate supplier
claims.requirementOrConstraint: The team needed to decide whether to swap the incumbent cup supplier for a candidate vendor on production grippers, using a plan fixed up front so 90 days of field data would map to adopt, reject or limited deployment.
claims.method: I designed every test in both phases. The plan sets the test conditions (weights, surfaces, slip sheet), measurement procedures, intervention triggers, the failure summary format, and the logic that maps Phase 2 results to an adopt, reject or limited-deployment recommendation.
claims.resultMetric: Reviewed, issued and used as the protocol for the field A/B I led at a 24/7 customer distribution center. That test caught the cracking at one site within about two weeks, before any fleet-wide rollout.
claims.limitations:
The System Configurations table leaves placeholders for the candidate vendor's specs (lip style, diameter, filter pairing), so the issued plan is incomplete without the vendor's input. Changes made during testing, like the extended tight stretch-wrap weights, aren't in it. It doesn't name who runs the analysis or with what tools. The team that owned post-test analysis did that informally. Phase 1 had no cyclic wear test, so the cracking first showed up in the field.
Next: add a cyclic wear test to Phase 1, and turn the open-ended vendor-input section (Section 6) into a structured feedback loop.

claims.title: Set the decision rule before any data came in
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Without a rule fixed in advance, a close result can drift into indefinite deferral or get adopted on the strength of the vendor relationship. The rule had to cover a clear win, a clear loss and a mixed result, and weigh both safety and productivity.
claims.method: I made it a two-condition rule. Piece loss rate per pick, the customer-facing safety metric, can't get worse than the incumbent's. And the candidate has to clear a threshold set in advance on at least one of four metrics: pick issues rate, order cycle issues rate, direct robot throughput, or downtime per intervention. I made a mixed result fall back to limited deployment under stated conditions, instead of forcing a yes or no. Two of the four metrics weren't standard StatsMonitor outputs yet, so I added them.
claims.resultMetric: The criteria were fixed before any data came in, and staging kept the failure to one site. The candidate cups cracked and wore down within about two weeks. After my internship ended, Mujin's on-site team applied the criteria and called a no-swap. The two new metrics stay in StatsMonitor as standard outputs for future qualifications.
claims.limitations:
I set the must-win threshold by engineering judgment, not from the incumbent's baseline variance. The must-win side is an OR across four metrics by design, so one metric clearing the bar can justify adoption even if the others are flat or slightly worse. The rule is performance-only and leaves out switching cost.
Next: calibrate the threshold to the incumbent's normal window-to-window variance from a pre-trial baseline, and to its historical wear and intervention data once that's compiled. If the OR gives ambiguous calls, try an AND or a weighted score. Add switching cost if the rule is reused for more expensive components.

claims.title: Designed the field triage and intervention protocol
claims.requirementOrConstraint: The 90-day decision is only as good as its maintenance data, so each failure mode (cup damage, filter clogging, blow-off solenoid fault) needed a predefined action, and the log had to stay comparable across both grippers and roll up into rates.
claims.method: I designed a backpressure check to tell a torn cup from a clogged filter or a blow-off solenoid fault. It fires the blow-off channels for a zone of cups with the mouths sealed. If pressure doesn't build, the next inspection step follows. I tied it to a fixed pick-count and time schedule, so the check runs without judgment calls in the field. I designed the replacement decision tree to tie a cleaning, a filter change or a cup swap to specific observed conditions, and set up the Service Log to record timestamp, intervention type and downtime minutes, which roll up into the normalized rates the gate uses.
claims.resultMetric: The triage protocol is in the issued plan, and the Service Log template went to the customer site with it as part of the A/B deployment package.
claims.limitations:
The blow-off schedule came from engineering judgment and rough priors from the incumbent's wear, and wasn't rigorously back-tested against historical Service Log data. The check wasn't validated on a known-fault gripper before deployment. The decision tree assumes failures show up at scheduled inspections, and intermittent ones, like a partial seal on one kind of surface, may not.
Next: test the check on a deliberately torn cup and a deliberately clogged filter to measure false-negative and false-positive rates. Calibrate the schedule against real field wear. If telemetry resolution allows, add per-cup vacuum-trace anomaly detection for intermittent failures.

claims.title: Ran the Phase 1 bench tests and found a failure on loose stretch-wrap
claims.requirementOrConstraint: Find failure modes like surface-dependent grip loss and weight limits on the bench, before the cup runs on a production gripper at a customer site for a long field window.
claims.method: I modified the force/vacuum test jig and ran the tests on it over about 2 days, with a KEYENCE digital pressure sensor. For each surface and each weight from 2 to 10 lb, I sealed the cup on the package and recorded steady vacuum and pull-off force. Then I held the vacuum module, cup and package in the air for 10 seconds, read vacuum at 5 and 10 seconds, and noted any slip, seal break or drop. A pass meant an unbroken seal and at most 10% vacuum decay from the steady level. I ran 2 to 3 trials per cell on the standard surfaces, and took tight stretch-wrap past the planned weight cap. Manufactured-weight packages weren't available at the higher weights, so I used real product samples in the target range. That kept real surfaces but put the weights slightly off-grid.
claims.resultMetric: Passed on new and damaged corrugate and slip sheet across the standard range. Failed on loose stretch-wrap, with vacuum decay past the limit and drops. Marginal on tight stretch-wrap above the planned weight cap, with a lift failure at the heaviest weight tested. The loose stretch-wrap failure mode went into Phase 2 as a documented known risk, and the on-site team and I watched for it. Phase 2 is observational and the customer controls the SKU mix, so the finding didn't change site operations.
claims.limitations:
No clean incumbent cups were available, so only the candidate was bench-tested. By design, Phase 1 checks absolute pass criteria and leaves the comparison to the system-level A/B in Phase 2. But a clean baseline would show whether the loose stretch-wrap failure is a regression or shared by both cups. Single-cup static tests don't reproduce multi-cup load sharing or robot motion, and the issued plan says so.
Next: re-run Phase 1 with a clean incumbent cup for a direct bench A/B. Before any future field deployment, test a partial zone of cups on a gripper to see whether neighboring cups mask the loose stretch-wrap failure.

outcome: I led the field A/B at a 24/7 customer distribution center. The candidate cups cracked and wore down within about two weeks. After my internship ended, Mujin's on-site team applied the plan's criteria and decided not to switch. The staged plan caught the failure at one site before a fleet-wide swap. Two of its metrics were added to StatsMonitor, my fleet monitoring pipeline.

projectRisks: Phase 1 tested only the candidate, statically and briefly, against absolute pass criteria. It couldn't show durability or compare cups, and no clean baseline cup was sourced this round.
Thresholds came from engineering judgment, with no historical baseline data on the incumbent. That's acceptable for a first version, but v2 should tighten them with real baseline variance.
Vendor specs are deliberately left as placeholders for the candidate vendor to fill in, which leaves gaps for anyone reproducing the tests from the plan alone.

I handed off on the last day of my internship without a formal transition document to walk a successor through the plan's unstated design decisions, including how its metrics tie into the StatsMonitor additions.

lessons.text: Staging kept a bad cup at one site instead of the fleet. A v2 plan should add what the bench lacked: a cyclic wear test, and a multi-cup test on part of a gripper for failures that neighboring cups hide.

Get clean baseline cups while writing the plan, not while running it. Without a paired incumbent run, Phase 1 could characterize the candidate but couldn't tell a regression from a weakness both cups share.

Name the analyst and analysis tools in the plan, not just the metrics. I left it implicit that field data goes to StatsMonitor, so someone inheriting the plan wouldn't know the pipeline is meant to consume it.
